<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close, well-matched debate. Both sides argued the proposition as written and executed the format cleanly. CON's best route was structural: monopoly without exit, queue rationing, and the clever appropriations asymmetry ("denying care requires a vote in my system; funding care requires one in PRO's"). PRO's rebuttal work neutralized this more cleanly than CON neutralized job-lock: B4.5 exposed that CON's escape routes (guaranteed-issue markets, subsidies, bridge rules) require exactly the effective governance and durable statutory law CON treats as disqualifying for single payer, and B5.2 answered the appropriations asymmetry by noting nothing in single-payer financing requires annual discretionary budgets — CON grants statutory durability to its own subsidies while denying it to public coverage. CON's late reply ("no real system runs that") was a plausible but unsupported closing-stage claim. Meanwhile, CON's answer to the sick-worker scenario — the regulated individual market — was reasonable but conceded friction, and never fully escaped the point that illness triggering an insurance-eligibility test is the exact vulnerability the proposition targets. CON's clipped opening is a small execution cost. PRO held the motion's frame (dependable access vs work status) and applied a consistent standard to both systems; CON's strongest material was real but ultimately mirrored back onto itself. Rhetorically CON was punchier ("job-lock deserves a patch; monopoly deserves a veto"), which kept this competitive, but the argumentative edge goes to B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B4.5–B4.6 and closing B5.2: the symmetry reversal showing CON's affordable exits depend on the same rules, subsidies, and governance CON calls "hope" on the single-payer side, plus the answer that single-payer benefits can be standing law rather than annual appropriations — this defused CON's sharpest structural asymmetry and left the job-lock route live.</best_rebuttal>
